summary.en: Being targeted because of where you, or people think you, come from.

recognise.en: "Jokes", nicknames or comments about someone's country, language or accent.
Being told to "go home", or that you are taking someone's place.
Being left out of study groups, housing or teams because of your nationality.
Students or staff demanding to see your papers when that is not their job.
Threats, damage to your things, or violence.

text.en: In your res kitchen, someone tells a student from Zimbabwe that "foreigners take our places". A few people laugh.

feedback.en: Staying in with the group can feel safer, and many people do it. But laughter tells the person targeted that they are alone, and tells the speaker it was fine.
This is safe, and it matters. Being asked "are you okay?" is often what people remember most.
Short and calm works best. You don't have to win the argument, and you should only do this if you feel safe.

you.en: It is not your fault, and you do not have to prove you belong.
Write down what happened, when, and who saw it, in case you want it later.
Talk to someone you trust: a friend, a mentor, a counsellor.
You can report it to your residence head, the equity or transformation office, or the international students office. Whether and when is your choice.
If you are threatened or in danger, go to campus security or the police straight away.

friend.en: Listen and believe them. Ask what they would like to happen next.
Include them: sit with them, invite them, walk with them.
Offer to go with them if they decide to report.
Don't confront an aggressive group on your own. Get help instead.

rights.en: The Constitution's equality clause protects everyone in South Africa from unfair discrimination, not only citizens.
On campus, look for: the equity or transformation office, the international students office, your residence head, the SRC and campus security.
Off campus, you can lay a complaint with the South African Human Rights Commission, or with the police if there are threats or violence.

summary.en: Any sexual act without consent. It is never the fault of the person it happened to.

recognise.en: Consent has to be freely given, and it can be withdrawn at any point.
Someone who is very drunk, drugged, asleep, frightened or pressured cannot consent.
It is most often done by someone the person knows: a friend, a partner, a classmate.
Freezing or not fighting back is a common reaction. It is not consent.
Being in a relationship, or having said yes before, is not consent.
Anyone can do it, and it can happen to anyone: women, men and non-binary people.

text.en: A friend tells you that someone she knows had sex with her when she was too drunk to say no. She says, "Maybe it was my fault."

feedback.en: Questions about drinking or clothes sound like blame, even when you mean well. Nothing she did makes it her fault.

label.en: Say "I believe you. It wasn't your fault."

feedback.en: These are the words survivors say helped most. You don't need to fix anything; being believed is the help.

label.en: Tell her she must report it

feedback.en: Reporting is her choice. Pressure takes control away again; offering options, and to go with her, gives it back.

you.en: It was not your fault, whatever you were wearing, drinking or doing.
Get to a place where you feel safe, and tell someone you trust if you can.
Medical care matters and some of it is time-sensitive: medicine to prevent HIV works best when started as soon as possible, within 72 hours, and emergency contraception is also available.
You can get medical care and counselling without opening a police case.
If you think you may want to report, try not to wash, and keep your clothes in a paper bag. You can still report later if you did wash.
Reporting is your choice, at your pace: to the university, to the police, to both, or to neither.

friend.en: Believe them, and say so. Listen without pressing for details.
Ask what they need, and offer to go with them to the clinic, counselling or the police.
Keep it confidential. It is their story to tell.
Supporting someone is heavy. Counselling is there for you too.

rights.en: You have the right to medical care, to be treated with dignity, and to report at any police station at any time.
On campus, look for: the campus clinic, student counselling, the gender-based violence or equity office, and campus security.
Thuthuzela Care Centres, at some public hospitals, offer medical care, counselling and legal support in one place.

summary.en: Drugs or extra alcohol added to a drink without the person knowing.

recognise.en: Feeling far more drunk than what you drank can explain.
Sudden dizziness, confusion, nausea, sleepiness or gaps in your memory.
A drink that tastes, smells or looks different.
It includes someone pouring you much stronger drinks than you agreed to.
It can happen to anyone, of any gender, at any kind of event.

text.en: At a party, your friend has had two drinks and suddenly can barely stand. Someone she met tonight offers to "take her home".

feedback.en: Someone who is suddenly very unwell should only leave with people she already trusts. This is exactly the moment spiking is meant to create.

label.en: Stay with her and leave together

feedback.en: Yes. Don't leave her alone, find the friends you came with, and get her somewhere safe.
The right call if she is getting worse, can't stay awake or is struggling to breathe. Tell them you think her drink was spiked.

you.en: Tell someone you trust straight away, and stay with them.
Don't leave alone, or with someone you have just met.
Get medical help if you feel very unwell. You can say you think you were spiked.
If there are gaps in your memory afterwards, medical care and counselling are available, and it was not your fault.

friend.en: Stay with them. Don't let them leave with someone they don't know well.
Get them somewhere safe and tell the venue or security.
If they pass out or struggle to breathe, call for medical help.
Go together, leave together, and plan the ride home before you go out.
Watch your drink being poured, and keep it with you.

rights.en: Spiking someone's drink is a crime, even if nothing else happens.
On campus, look for: campus security, the campus clinic, student counselling and your residence head.
You can report it to the venue, the university or the police. Getting medical help comes first.

summary.en: Being treated worse, or shut out, because of your race, language, religion or background.

recognise.en: "Jokes", stereotypes or comments about your race, hair, accent or language.
Being ignored, marked down or doubted when others are not.
Being left out of groups, residences or opportunities because of who you are.
Being told you only got in because of your race or your funding.

text.en: In a group project, two members keep giving your friend the "easy" tasks and talk over her. One says, "We just want it done properly."

feedback.en: It can feel like it isn't your place. But silence from the rest of the group is usually read as agreement.
"I'd like to hear her idea" is small, safe and effective. It changes the room without starting a fight.

label.en: Ask her what she wants to do

feedback.en: This keeps the choice with her. She may want support in the group, a word with the lecturer, or just to be heard.

you.en: What happened is about them, not about your worth or your place here.
Keep a record: dates, words used, who was there, and any messages or marks.
Talk it through with someone you trust before deciding what to do.
You can raise it informally with a lecturer or residence head, or formally with the equity or transformation office. It is your choice.

friend.en: Believe them. Don't explain it away or ask whether they are "sure".
Say something in the moment if it is safe, or check in with them afterwards.
Offer to be a witness, or to go with them if they report.

rights.en: The Constitution prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds including race, ethnic origin, language, religion and culture.
On campus, look for: the equity or transformation office, the dean of students, your residence head and the SRC.
Off campus, you can complain to the South African Human Rights Commission or use an Equality Court, which sits at magistrates' courts.

title.en: Sexual harassment, including by people in power

summary.en: Unwanted sexual attention, including from a lecturer, tutor, supervisor or residence leader.

recognise.en: Sexual comments, messages, "jokes" or staring that you did not ask for.
Unwanted touching, or someone who keeps asking after you have said no.
Hints that marks, a reference, a room or a job depend on going along with it.
It is still harassment if you laughed, froze or did not say no clearly.
The person doing it can be a man or a woman, and so can the person it is done to.

text.en: A tutor who marks your friend's work messages him late at night, comments on his body, and suggests he "discuss his marks" at her flat.

feedback.en: Jokes like this are why many men never report. She has power over his marks, he didn't ask for it, and it is harassment.
Screenshots and a trusted friend give him options later, whatever he decides. He doesn't have to act today.
He can ask the harassment or equity office how the process works, and what protection he would have, before deciding anything.

you.en: It is not your fault, and you are not overreacting.
Keep the evidence: messages, emails, dates, and anyone who saw or heard.
You can ask for a different tutor or supervisor while it is being dealt with.
You can get confidential advice first, and decide about a formal report later.

friend.en: Take it seriously. Don't joke about it or tell them to "just block the person".
Offer to go with them to the office or to counselling.
Don't confront the person or spread it. That can make things harder for your friend.

rights.en: You have the right to study without sexual harassment, and staff who abuse their position can be disciplined or dismissed.
On campus, look for: the sexual harassment or gender-based violence office, the equity office, student counselling and the SRC.
The Protection from Harassment Act lets you apply for a protection order at a magistrate's court.

summary.en: Control, threats or violence from a partner or ex-partner. It is not only physical.

recognise.en: Checking your phone, deciding who you see, or cutting you off from friends and family.
Insults, humiliation, threats, or blaming you for their anger.
Taking or controlling your money, allowance or bank card.
Pushing, hitting, or pressuring you into sex.
Apologies and promises that are followed by the same thing again.
It happens in all kinds of relationships, and the person doing it can be of any gender.

text.en: Your friend's girlfriend goes through his phone, decides who he can see, and slaps him when she is angry. He laughs it off: "It's nothing."

feedback.en: Men are often expected to shrug this off, which keeps it hidden. Being hit and controlled by a partner is abuse, whoever does it.
Naming what you see, without judging him, is one of the most useful things a friend can do. Then keep the door open.
Isolation is how control works. Staying in his life, and making sure he has a number to call, keeps his options open.

you.en: You don't deserve it, and you did not cause it.
Tell one person you trust what is really happening.
Think about safety first: somewhere you could go, a bag ready, a number saved under another name.
Counsellors and the helplines will talk through options without pushing you to leave or to report.

friend.en: Listen without judging, and don't give ultimatums.
Keep inviting them, even when they keep saying no.
If you think they are in immediate danger, call campus security or the police.

rights.en: The Domestic Violence Act covers dating relationships too, and lets you apply for a protection order at a magistrate's court.
Controlling someone's money, and emotional abuse, count as abuse under the law, not only violence.
On campus, look for: student counselling, the gender-based violence office, campus security and your residence head.

summary.en: Being targeted or shut out because of who you love or your gender identity.

recognise.en: Slurs, "jokes" or mocking the way someone speaks, dresses or moves.
Outing someone, or threatening to.
Refusing to use someone's name, or shutting them out of rooms, teams or events.
Being told it is "un-African" or a phase, or being preached at.
Threats and violence, including sexual violence.

text.en: Someone in your corridor finds out a first-year is gay and starts telling others. People go quiet when he walks into the kitchen.

feedback.en: Neutral feels safe, but to the person being frozen out it looks the same as joining in.

label.en: Treat him as you always have

feedback.en: Greeting him, sitting with him and using his name is quiet, and it is powerful. It shows others what normal looks like.
"That's his business, leave it" is enough. Outing someone can put them in real danger at home and on campus.

you.en: There is nothing wrong with you.
You decide who knows, and when. Nobody has the right to out you.
Look for your people: most campuses have a society for LGBTQI+ students and allies.
If you are threatened or unsafe where you live, ask the residence office about moving, and tell campus security.

friend.en: Thank them for trusting you, and keep it to yourself.
Use the name and pronouns they ask for.
Speak up when they are not in the room, too.

rights.en: The Constitution prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender and sex.
On campus, look for: the equity or transformation office, student counselling, the residence office and LGBTQI+ student societies.
Threats and assault are crimes, and can be reported to the police.

summary.en: Being left out because campus, teaching or people don't make room for your disability or health condition.

recognise.en: Venues, residences or transport you can't get into or use.
Notes, slides, tests or online systems in a format you can't access.
Being refused extra time, a scribe, captions or other support you need.
Being treated as a burden, or doubted because the condition is not visible.
It includes mental health conditions, chronic illness and learning differences.

text.en: A classmate with a hearing impairment misses half of every lecture because the lecturer faces the board and posts no notes. She is thinking of dropping the module.

feedback.en: Kind, and it helps today. It also leaves the real problem in place for her and for the next student.

label.en: Go with her to the disability unit

feedback.en: The unit can arrange notes, captions or seating and speak to the lecturer for her. That is what it is there for.
She knows her needs best. Asking, instead of assuming, is the respectful place to start.

you.en: Needing an adjustment is not asking for a favour.
Register with the disability unit early, even if you are not sure you will need it. It is confidential.
Ask for what you need in writing, and keep the replies.
If a lecturer refuses an agreed adjustment, the disability unit or faculty can step in.

friend.en: Ask before helping, and listen to the answer.
Choose venues and plans everyone can get to.
Back them up when they ask for an adjustment.

rights.en: The Constitution prohibits unfair discrimination on the ground of disability, and universities are expected to provide reasonable accommodation.
On campus, look for: the disability unit, your faculty office, student counselling and the exams office for test arrangements.
If the university does not respond, you can complain to the South African Human Rights Commission.

summary.en: "Traditions" that humiliate, hurt or endanger new students, and pressure to go along with them.

recognise.en: Being forced to drink, stay awake, do exercises or run errands for seniors.
Humiliating tasks, nicknames, uniforms or rules that only first-years must follow.
Being told it is "voluntary" when refusing has consequences.
Secrecy: being told not to tell anyone, or not to film.
Threats of being left out of the house or its events if you don't take part.

text.en: At 2am, the senior women in your res wake your corridor for a "welcome tradition": first-years must drink and do push-ups in the quad. Your roommate looks terrified.

label.en: Go along so you fit in

feedback.en: The pressure to belong is real, and many people go along. Belonging that depends on being humiliated is not a fair price.
Saying no is easier with one other person. You are allowed to refuse, and you don't owe anyone a reason.

label.en: Report it to the residence head

feedback.en: Most universities ban these practices, and reports can usually be made without your name. It protects next year's first-years too.

you.en: You are allowed to say no, and to leave.
If you are hurt or made to drink too much, get medical help first.
Write down what happened, who led it and who was there.
You can report to the residence head, the residence office or Student Affairs, usually without giving your name.

friend.en: Stick together, and leave together.
Don't film or share someone being humiliated.
When you are a senior, be the one who stops it.

rights.en: Most universities ban initiation practices, and "tradition" is not a defence.
Forcing someone to drink, or hurting them, can be assault, which is a crime.
On campus, look for: your residence head, the residence office, Student Affairs and campus security.

title.en: Online abuse, including sharing intimate images

summary.en: Harassment, threats or humiliation through phones and social media.

recognise.en: Sharing, or threatening to share, private photos or videos of you.
Being pressured to send nudes, or blackmailed with ones you sent.
Fake accounts, edited images, rumours or group chats made to shame you.
Constant messages, tracking your location, or logging into your accounts.

text.en: After a break-up, your friend's ex-girlfriend threatens to post private photos of him in the res WhatsApp group unless he takes her back.

label.en: Tell him not to have sent them

feedback.en: Trusting a partner is not the offence. Threatening to share the photos is, and blame makes it harder for him to ask for help.
Screenshots of the threats, with dates and her number, matter if he decides to report. Then block and report the account.

label.en: Go with him to get help

feedback.en: Threatening to share intimate images is a crime, whoever does it. Campus offices and the police can act, and he should not have to face it alone.

you.en: It is not your fault, even if you sent the image yourself.
Don't pay or give in to blackmail. It usually does not stop there.
Save the evidence before you block: screenshots, usernames, dates.
Report the content to the platform so it can be taken down, and tell someone you trust.

friend.en: Don't open, forward or save the images. Sharing them again adds to the harm.
Report the post or group, and say something if it is safe.
Stay with your friend. Shame grows when people go quiet.

rights.en: Sharing someone's intimate images without consent, or threatening to, is a crime in South Africa.
The Protection from Harassment Act covers online harassment, and lets you apply for a protection order.
On campus, look for: the gender-based violence office, student counselling, campus security and the IT help desk for account security.
